text:
alex: Hey team, can we put together a short customer-facing playbook for Private/VPC deploys when GPU pools hit capacity ceilings? Customers keep asking what to do on their side to reduce tail latency and prevent big queue growth.

maya: +1. they want concrete ingress-side patterns — not just "retry less". Ideally a few options with tradeoffs (latency vs throughput vs cost).

sam: I wrote something similar for hosted but private has networking + burst constraints. Quick sketch: 1) client-side admission control (token bucket), 2) adaptive concurrency limits, 3) prioritized request classes + soft-degradation, 4) graceful retry headers + backoff hints.

jules: Agree. Also include an example Envoy/NGINX snippet and a minimal SDK change to expose server backpressure headers. Customers love copy-paste.

alex: Cool. Draft section ideas: "When you see saturation", "How to detect it from your side", "Immediate mitigations", "Medium-term changes", "Example configs + SDK hints". I'll start a short root msg and we can iterate.

maya: Detection checklist (client-side):
- rising 95/99p response times
- queueing observed in logs (long request wait time before wire write)
- 429 / 503 rate spikes correlated with busy GPUs
- infra-bot capacity alerts (e.g., `infra-bot: private-gpu-pool-us-west: saturated`)

sam: Immediate mitigations (low-risk, no infra changes):
- apply client-side rate shaping: token-bucket with burst=2x baseline, refill based on sustained throughput.
- add per-route concurrency limit (max in-flight requests per connection).
- enable per-request timeout and drop long-hanging requests early.
- return quick 429 with Retry-After when local queue > threshold.

jules: Example token-bucket pseudo-config (recommended defaults):
```
# client-side
bucket_capacity = 50
refill_rate_per_sec = 10
burst_allowed = 2.0
# if queue_length > 100 -> switch to conservative mode: refill_rate_per_sec /= 2
```
Add telemetry: emit metrics for allowed_vs_dropped and current_tokens.

sam: SDK behaviour suggestion: when server sends backpressure hint header X-RWBP=low|med|high, SDK should shrink token bucket and increase per-request timeouts. Example mapping:
- low -> multiply refill by 0.8
- med -> 0.5
- high -> 0.2 + respond with local 429 if tokens exhausted

maya: Graceful degradation patterns (medium-term):
- fallback to smaller model variant (if available) with approximation metric in responses.
- apply request prioritization: interactive user requests > background batch jobs. Use priority header.
- offload embeddings/batch ops to dedicated pools when possible.

alex: Network considerations specific to VPC/private:
- keep-alive and connection pooling reduce cold-start pressure on load balancers.
- avoid large concurrent POSTs over same connection; prefer multiple connections with concurrency cap in client.
- if using NAT gateways, watch for SNAT exhaustion under bursty fan-out.

jules: Envoy rate limit example (token bucket style using local rate limit):
```
http_filters:
- name: envoy.filters.http.local_ratelimit
  typed_config:
    '@type': type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.local_ratelimit.v3.LocalRateLimit
    stat_prefix: http_local_rate_limiter
    token_bucket:
      max_tokens: 20
      tokens_per_fill: 5
      fill_interval: 1s
    filter_enabled:
      runtime_key: local_rate_limit_enabled
```
Note: tune tokens_per_fill relative to expected per-second QPS and model latency.

sam: On the server-side we will emit these headers so SDKs can react: X-RWBP-Level (low|med|high), X-RWBP-Queue (current queue length), X-RWBP-EstLat (ms). Add guidance: if X-RWBP-Level=high, clients should reduce concurrency by at least 50% for 30s.

maya: Retry strategy guidance:
- immediate 429: short exponential backoff with jitter, max attempts 3 for interactive flows.
- 503: treat as transient but backoff longer (initial 250ms -> 500ms -> 1s).
- avoid aggressive retries on batched jobs; prefer requeue semantics with a worker that respects rate tokens.

alex: Cost/throughput tradeoffs to call out:
- tighter client-side shaping reduces tail latency but may increase apparent SLA misses (more 429s).
- soft-degrade (smaller models) trades quality for throughput — measurable with eval sets.
- batching increases throughput/cost efficiency but raises latency variance; expose batch window in client config.

jules: Quick paste for README snippet customers can copy into their SDK layer:
```
# pseudocode
while true:
  if tokens.try_consume(1):
    resp = call_redwood(request, timeout=5s)
    if resp.headers['X-RWBP-Level']=='high':
      tokens.scale(0.5) # chill for a bit
  else:
    sleep(random_backoff())
```

sam: Logs/telemetry to ask customers to share when debugging:
- client-side allowed_vs_dropped counts, current_token_level
- observed Retry-After and X-RWBP-* headers
- 95/99p latency for each route, and backlog length in their gateway
- NAT gateway metrics if applicable

maya: Want to include a short decision matrix: when to ask us to add capacity vs when to change client config.
- add capacity: sustained QPS above committed baseline, business-critical SLA breaches, model upgrade requiring more GPU.
- client changes: transient spikes, noisy neighbors on multi-tenant pools, customers with mixed workloads (batch + interactive).

alex: This is great. I'll clean and format into a 1-pager playbook and a small snippet pack for support. Can we also get infra to emit the X-RWBP headers from private control-plane by default?@infra-bot any objections?

infra-bot: infra-bot: queued task registered: enable-rwbp-headers for private control plane can be rolled as a config flag. Expect a canary next week.

jules: Nice. Final ask: include an example NGINX limit_req config too for customers on a simple proxy.

sam: I'll add that and send PR to the docs repo.

alex: Thanks all — I'll drop the cleaned playbook in #docs once done. :thumbsup:
